Learning outcomes
  1. Identify which roots are surds (irrational) and which simplify to rational numbers..
  2. Apply the surd laws to simplify expressions.
  3. Apply the index laws to simplify expressions.
``` ## Surds - A surd is an exact [irrational root](002_simplify_brackets.qmd#real-numbers) expession that cannot be simplified to a [rational number](002_simplify_brackets.qmd#real-numbers). - Examples: $\sqrt{2},\ \sqrt{3},\ \sqrt[3]{6}$. - $\sqrt{9}$ is not a surd because it can be further simplified to $3$, which is a rational number. - Types: - Pure: have a single irrational root, e.g., $\sqrt{2},\ \sqrt{3},\ \sqrt[3]{6}$. - Mixed: have a rational number and an irrational root, e.g., $3\sqrt{2}$. ### Surd laws 1. $\sqrt{ab} = \sqrt{a}\sqrt{b}$, for $a,b\ge0$. 2. $\sqrt{a}\sqrt{a} = a$, for $a\ge0$. 3. $\displaystyle \sqrt{\frac{a}{b}} = \frac{\sqrt{a}}{\sqrt{b}}$, for $a\ge0$ and $b>0$. 4. $\sqrt{a}\pm\sqrt{b}\ne\sqrt{a\pm b}$ in general. 5. $\displaystyle \sqrt[n]{a} = a^{1/n}$ whenever both sides are defined as real numbers. ```{=html}
Worked Examples & Practice
``` :::: panel-tabset ## Example M.4.1 {{< iconify ic:round-menu-book size=21px >}} Simplify: $\displaystyle \boldsymbol{\sqrt{28}}$ $$ \begin{aligned} \sqrt{28} &= \sqrt{4 \times 7} \\ &= \sqrt{4} \sqrt{7} \\ &= \boxed{2\sqrt{7}} \end{aligned} $$ ## Example M.4.2 {{< iconify ic:round-menu-book size=21px >}} Simplify: $\displaystyle \boldsymbol{\sqrt{\frac{52}{9}}}$ $$ \begin{aligned} \sqrt{\frac{52}{9}} &=\frac{\sqrt{52}}{\sqrt{9}}\\ &=\frac{\sqrt{4 \times 13}}{3}\\ &=\frac{\sqrt{4} \sqrt{13}}{3}\\ &=\boxed{\frac{2}{3}\sqrt{13}} \end{aligned} $$ ## [Exercise M.4.1 {{< iconify fluent:chat-bubbles-question-20-filled size=21px >}}]{style="color: #ba181b"} For each of the following roots, indicate whether it is surd or not: ::: {.webex-check .webex-box} $\sqrt{25}$ $\sqrt{35}$ $\sqrt{67}$ $\sqrt[3]{8}$ ::: :::: ## Indices - An index (known also as exponent) is the power to which a base is raised. - It indicates how many times the base is multiplied by itself. - For example $4^2$, $4$ is the base and $2$ is the index (it is read as **four squared** or **four raised to the power two**). ### Index laws 1. $a^m \times a^n = a^{m+n}$ 2. $\displaystyle \frac{a^m}{a^n} = a^{m-n}$, for $a\ne0$ 3. $\displaystyle a^{-m} =\frac{1}{a^m}$, for $a\ne0$ 4. $(a^m)^n = a^{mn}$ 5. $\left( a^mb^n \right)^k = a^{mk} \times b^{nk}$ 6. $a^1=a$ 7. 7. $a^0=1$, for $a\ne0$ ```{=html}
Worked Examples & Practice
``` ::: panel-tabset ## Example M.4.3 {{< iconify ic:round-menu-book size=21px >}} Simplify: $\displaystyle \boldsymbol{\frac{x^6}{x^2}}$ $$ \frac{x^6}{x^2} = x^{6-2} = \boxed{x^4} $$ ## Example M.4.4 {{< iconify ic:round-menu-book size=21px >}} Simplify: $\displaystyle \boldsymbol{16^{3/4}}$ $$ \begin{aligned} 16^{3/4} &= \left( 16^{1/4} \right)^3 \\ &= \left( \sqrt[4]{16} \right)^3 \\ &= 2^3 \\ &= \boxed{8} \end{aligned} $$ ## [Exercise M.4.2 {{< iconify fluent:chat-bubbles-question-20-filled size=21px >}}]{style="color: #ba181b"} Simplify: $\displaystyle \boldsymbol{y^3(y^{-2}-y^{-3})}$ The answer is ## [Exercise M.4.3 {{< iconify fluent:chat-bubbles-question-20-filled size=21px >}}]{style="color: #ba181b"} Use the R code block below to calculate the following expression: $\displaystyle \boldsymbol{\frac{27^{1/3} \times 9^{1/2}}{3^{-1}}}$ ```{webr-r} # Write your R code here then click "Run Code" to print the answer ```
